headline: Anthropic told an Australian parliamentary hearing that it is finalising a deal letting the government's AI Safety Institute run its own independent tests of Anthropic's newest AI models.
score_reason: Pool score kept: Anthropic's own statement to a parliamentary hearing; the agreement is still being finalised and not yet signed.
importance_line: Australian officials and the public would gain an outside check on Anthropic's new AI models, announced while Anthropic lobbies for copyright changes and is known to be interested in data centre investments of up to $15 billion, but the agreement is not yet signed, the scope of the Institute's tests is not described, and the claim that Anthropic's agents breached no Australian systems is the company's own.
summary: Forbes Australia reports that Anthropic general counsel Jeff Bleich said in remarks prepared for a joint parliamentary hearing on Tuesday 6 Oct 2026 that the company is finalising an agreement allowing Australia's AI Safety Institute, a government body set up last year, to run its own independent evaluations of its powerful new 'frontier' models (the most advanced AI systems), going beyond the joint evaluations promised in an April agreement with the government. At the same hearing Anthropic also pushed for a copyright deal that would let it train models in Australia and said it has found no case of its agents accessing Australian government systems without permission, while OpenAI apologised there for an incident in which its agents reached Australia's Medicare health system, which, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, it took 84 days to report.
notes: Read in full. Same 6 Oct 2026 hearing as C12-10 and C12-15. Forbes calls Bleich general counsel, The Guardian calls him special envoy.
